name: Dog Coat Colour Calculator
seoTitle: Dog Coat Colour Calculator — Formula & Results
seoDesc: Dog coat colour comes from four genes acting in a fixed order: E, K, B and D. Free dog coat colour calculator: enter your values and get loci answered instant
summary:
Dog coat colour comes from four genes acting in a fixed order: E, K, B and D. It returns loci answered, and the panel shows all of them at once.

This page takes the genotype at those four loci and returns the colour you would see, the full gene order, and what each locus is doing. Every result is derived from the boxes you fill in, so changing one input updates the whole panel at once. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Dog Coat Colour
sections.html:
E → K → B → D, in that order: E decides if black is made, K overrides the agouti pattern, B sets black vs brown, D dilutes whatever pigment is left

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
Eextension — e/e blocks all black pigmentlocus
Kdominant black: K^B solid, K^br brindle, k^y allows agoutilocus
Bb/b turns black pigment brownlocus
Dd/d dilutes black to blue and brown to lilaclocus

sections.title: How do I use the Dog Coat Colour?
sections.html:
The form asks only for what the formula needs — nothing is optional decoration.

  1. Enter the genotype at each locus — a dog can only be E/E or E/e if it shows any black at all.
  2. Tick ticking if the dog has flecks on its white areas; that is the T locus and it is not part of the four-locus colour model.
  3. Read the predicted colour, then the gene-order explanation: it tells you which locus is actually responsible, which is what matters if you are planning a litter.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: ticking or roan spotting (t locus) of 0.

The arithmetic is the page's own: change one box and the result moves by the amount the formula implies, which is the quickest way to convince yourself the tool is honest.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
A raw figure only means something next to the bands it is normally judged against. Here is the scale that goes with this one:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
e/eRed, yellow or creamno black pigment can be made, whatever the other loci say
E/- + K^BSolid blackdominant black overrides the agouti pattern
E/- + k^y/k^y + B/-Black, or agouti if A allowsthe A locus decides the pattern
b/bChocolate or liverblack pigment turned brown
d/dBlue, lilac or isabelladilution of whatever the dog would otherwise be

  • The order matters and is the whole point of the page: a b/b dog that is also e/e is not chocolate, because with no black pigment there is nothing for B to turn brown. Epistasis runs E over K over A over B over D.

  • Dilution is a pigment-density effect, not a colour: d/d turns black into blue and brown into lilac, and dilutes red to a paler cream.

  • Two loci that often surprise people are missing from this model on purpose — the A (agouti) pattern, which needs a full allele series to be useful, and the merle locus, which is incompletely dominant and often unhealthy in homozygotes.

  • Locus notation varies by author (E, EXT; K, CBD103; B, TYRP1; D, MLPH). The phenotype is the same; the letters are convention.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
The arithmetic is simple; the inputs are where things go wrong. The usual culprits:

  • Naming a colour from the B locus alone: a b/b dog with no black pigment is red, not chocolate.
  • Assuming two chocolate parents give only chocolate puppies — they do, at the B locus, but E and K still decide whether any black pigment exists to be browned.
  • Breeding two merle dogs because the colours look interesting; double merle causes deafness and eye defects, which is why merle is not offered here.
  • Reading K^br as "any brindle pattern": brindle needs black pigment to stripe, so an e/e dog cannot be brindled.

faq.q: How is dog coat colour inherited?
faq.a: Through a small set of loci acting in a fixed order. E decides whether black pigment is produced at all; K overrides the agouti pattern with solid black or brindle; A sets the pattern; B makes black pigment brown; D dilutes the result.

faq.q: Can two black Labradors have yellow puppies?
faq.a: Yes — if both parents are E/e. The puppies that inherit e from both sides cannot make black pigment and are yellow, whatever their B and K loci say.

faq.q: What makes a dog chocolate instead of black?
faq.a: Two copies of b at the TYRP1 locus, plus at least one E so that black pigment is actually being made. Without E, the B locus has nothing to act on.
No. It predicts a phenotype from a genotype you enter. The loci are real and commercially tested, but a prediction from a pedigree is only as good as the assumed genotypes.

faq.q: What does the Dog Coat Colour actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns loci answered. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.
